title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc inferential sensitivity bound tied to the observed contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Translating operator intent into device configuration is a core NetOps activity. Large language models (LLMs) promise to accelerate intent→configuration workflows, but probabilistic generation introduces ordering errors, omissions, and unsafe commands. Prior proposals advocate guarded pipelines that pair probabilistic generators with deterministic validators/simulators and bounded repair loops as operational floor‑safety nets. However, rigorous preregistered evaluations that quantify how tightly bounded guarded pipelines change first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics remain limited.

We conducted a narrowly scoped, preregistered paired experiment to evaluate the incremental effect of a minimal guarded pipeline composed of (1) a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), (2) a frozen deterministic validator that canonicalizes and statically checks workflow constraints, and (3) at most one automated repair attempt when the validator reports violations. Our research question: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce the first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Contributions: (i) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and archived per‑task artifacts; (ii) confirmatory statistics derived from those artifacts; (iii) a compact post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to observed contingency counts; (iv) artifact‑grounded design recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations.
sections.related_work: LLM-based intent→configuration demonstrations and system papers show promising synthesis in lab settings but emphasize failure modes (misordering, omission, overconfidence) that threaten operational safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Work in adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) finds verifier‑assisted and retrieval‑augmented pipelines reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating guarded architectures for NetOps [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1,10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Established deterministic verification techniques (e.g., header‑space/specification checking) provide algorithmic foundations for static validators capable of policy and reachability checks without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Surveys and reviews underscore generate→verify→repair as a recommended pattern while highlighting auditability and human‑oversight concerns [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our study situates a preregistered paired evaluation at the intersection of these strands by measuring first‑pass validity under an explicit validator+repair floor.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 before observing final outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. Planning assumed baseline pass rate = 0.40, which informed sample‑size logic; that assumption is reported because it affects interpretation.

Design and sampling: Paired within‑task design with a deterministic seed list of 300 tasks (task IDs 0001–0300). For each seed a single LLM candidate was produced and used as the baseline response and as the starting point for guarded validation/repair (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Planned episodes = 600; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The shared‑candidate choice reflects an operational workflow (repair of a single proposed plan) but increases within‑pair correlation and limits informative discordant pairs for paired tests.

Model and provider settings: Declared generation model: gpt-5-mini. Execution accounting: model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial + 1 repair). The archived model configuration records the sampling temperature as null: execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa) contains "temperature": null. A null/unset temperature in that artifact is not evidence of deterministic sampling (temperature=0); sampling determinism was therefore unspecified in the archived configuration and generator variance may reflect nonfixed sampling settings. This concise artifact‑grounded disclosure matters for cross‑run variability and interpretive headroom for paired comparisons.

Validator and repair: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized outputs to a normalized AST and applied static workflow/dependency checks derived from task payloads. The scoring rule (full intent‑constraint validation) marks success only if required_sequence, expected_final_state, and workflow policies are satisfied. When violations are reported the preregistered repair adapter may be invoked once to apply minimal edits; repaired output is revalidated by the same validator. Validator traces record normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, and a boolean valid flag; these structured traces are the basis for repair triggers and scoring.

Contamination and missingness: Deterministic contamination detection used normalized‑AST equality and near‑duplicate thresholds; exact duplicates trigger preregistered deterministic replacement from a reserve set. Provider/infrastructure failures follow the preregistered retry policy (single retry); primary analysis uses 'complete_pair_primary' (drop pairs only if both calls failed). All exclusions/replacements and failed‑call events were recorded in the execution manifest.

Primary estimand and analysis: Primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary test = exact McNemar two‑sided (α=0.05); paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) for the absolute paired difference was preregistered. Secondary analyses included Clopper–Pearson CIs for repair success and stratified checks by task difficulty. All analytic code and artifacts are archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): planned episodes = 600; completed = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300; model_calls_used = 301; repair invocations = 1. No provider or infrastructure failures occurred; no preregistered contamination exclusions were required.

Primary outcomes (archived counts): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.6667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency from archived artifacts: n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0.

Inferential results (preregistered): Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Absolute paired difference = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Repair outcome (H2): the single allowed repair corrected the lone invalid baseline (repair success 1/1); Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0].

Post‑hoc sensitivity bound: The observed total discordant pairs = 1 bounds the resolvable absolute paired difference to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. Thus the preregistered planning target (≥50% relative reduction from planned baseline 0.40, implying ≈+0.30 absolute) was incompatible with the observed near‑ceiling baseline; ~90 net discordant pairs favoring guarded outputs would have been required to realize that planned absolute change for N=300. These numerical facts are reproduced directly from archived analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv).
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation: The archived contingency (n11=299,n10=1,n01=0,n00=0) constrains inference: absolute paired difference = (n10−n01)/N = 1/300 and any exact McNemar test conditions on the discordant count (1), yielding p=1.00. The paired bootstrap CI expresses the same limitation in interval form.

Design lessons: (1) Power planning must account for plausible baseline prevalence and pairing semantics: shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce discordant counts for a given marginal prevalence. (2) When repair effectiveness is a primary claim, preregister and ensure sufficient expected initial failures (by adjusting task difficulty or adversarial augmentation) to obtain a precise conditional estimate. (3) Deterministic validator traces (normalized_configuration, violation_codes, parsed/required_command_count) are essential for explainable failure‑mode analysis and reproducible post‑mortems.

Construct validity: Our validator performed static canonicalization/checks rather than dynamic emulation; runtime behaviors (control‑plane convergence, transient reachability) were not executed and remain unmeasured. For operational claims about runtime effects future studies should integrate emulation/simulation stages and preregister emulation‑to‑success mapping.

Operational implication: A frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded repair loop can correct individual invalid candidates (1/1 correction observed) and serve as a safety net. When baseline error prevalence is already rare, the primary operational value may be catastrophic‑risk mitigation rather than throughput improvement.

Reproducibility: All per‑task inputs, normalized responses, validator traces, repair prompts/responses, analysis code, and the execution manifest are archived and are the authoritative source for reported counts and intervals. The archived model configuration records the temperature field as null (see Methods and Disclosure) which limits claims about sampling determinism across runs.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline with a frozen deterministic validator and a single automated repair iteration. Baseline generation yielded 299/300 valid outputs and the guarded pipeline yielded 300/300 valid outputs. The single repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output, but the observed near‑ceiling baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and removed statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should (a) calibrate task difficulty or adversarially augment tasks to produce sufficient initial failures or discordant counts, (b) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly, and (c) include emulation when runtime semantic effects are material. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement for reproduction.

Preregistration: cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 (the preregistration record was created before observing final outcomes; preregistration SHA‑256 is recorded in the execution manifest). Declared model and tooling: gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version), adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1, frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Execution accounting (archived): planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair invocation), repair-stage invocations = 1. The execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle enumerate all raw model responses, per‑task validator traces (normalized configurations, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, repair_applied flags), repair prompts/responses, execution logs, and analysis artifacts; these archived artifacts are the authoritative source for the numeric counts and intervals reported in this manuscript.

Model configuration artifact disclosure required by review: the archived model configuration records the sampling temperature as null. Concretely, execution/model_configuration.json records "temperature": null (SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). A null/unset temperature entry in that artifact is not evidence of deterministic sampling (temperature=0); sampling determinism was therefore unspecified in the archived configuration and generator variance may reflect nonfixed sampling settings. We include this concise artifact‑grounded disclosure because sampling determinism affects cross‑run variability and interpretive headroom for paired comparisons.

The autonomous pipeline performed literature search, preregistration, execution, analysis, AI‑peer‑review style checks, and manuscript drafting autonomously after the autonomy lock in accordance with the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track requirements. The preregistered planning assumption used in power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) is explicitly reported because it materially affects interpretation of the confirmatory result. The archived execution manifest and analysis bundle are the authoritative artifacts for all reported counts, intervals, and hashes.
limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.

Model sampling temperature in the archived model configuration was recorded as null (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa); null/unset does not imply deterministic sampling (temperature=0) and sampling determinism was therefore unspecified.
